metadata.summary: Select corticosteroids for eligible severe AH, verify the regimen, reassess with Lille on day 4 or 7, and stop ineffective or unsafe exposure.
concepts: Original MELD and modified Maddrey DF
metadata.application: Calculate mDF with verified inputs, identify unresolved contraindications, and assign the response and safety reviews before treatment begins.
keyPoints: Severity and eligibility require separate assessment.
mDF uses PT minus laboratory control PT and bilirubin in mg/dL.
Lille is a timed treatment-response assessment.
Nonresponse and new serious hazards require action.

bodies.heading: Establish the syndrome and estimate severity
bodies.body: Confirm a compatible alcohol-associated hepatitis (AH) syndrome and evaluate competing causes before using a prognostic score to select treatment. The 2024 ACG guideline uses original MELD greater than 20 to define severe AH; the score alone does not establish the cause or corticosteroid eligibility. Benefit is not a simple function of increasing severity. ACG identifies the greatest corticosteroid benefit in the MELD 25 to 39 range and calls for careful risk-benefit review above 50. Very severe illness warrants urgent multidisciplinary assessment, not an automatic higher steroid dose.

bodies.heading: Calculate modified Maddrey DF with the correct inputs
bodies.body: The historical modified Maddrey discriminant function (mDF) is 4.6 × [patient prothrombin time − laboratory control prothrombin time] + total bilirubin. Use PT values in seconds and bilirubin in mg/dL; do not substitute INR for the PT difference or silently insert bilirubin reported in another unit. Worked example: patient PT 18 seconds, control PT 12 seconds and bilirubin 12 mg/dL give 4.6 × (18 − 12) + 12 = 39.6. The result exceeds the historical severe-AH threshold of at least 32. This complements clinical assessment; it neither proves AH nor overrides a contraindication. Laboratory-dependent PT limits comparisons across centers.

bodies.heading: Control hazards before starting treatment
bodies.body: Assess active infection, including untreated hepatitis B infection, uncontrolled diabetes, gastrointestinal bleeding and severe renal failure. These are corticosteroid contraindications in the ACG AH framework. Treat or control the problem and let the liver team reassess eligibility; adequately controlled infection, bleeding or renal dysfunction may permit later reconsideration rather than a permanent exclusion. Review other clinical hazards and the overall trajectory. Do not interpret an elevated MELD or mDF as permission to start steroids through an unresolved contraindication.

bodies.heading: Select an oral regimen within the liver-team plan
bodies.body: Prednisolone 40 mg orally each day is the commonly studied regimen for an eligible adult with severe AH, with a planned course of four weeks if response and safety permit. ACG also describes prednisone 40 mg/day, while noting that prednisolone has been more extensively studied and is generally used. The prescription needs an explicit response-review date and ongoing safety checks. Four weeks is a planned duration for appropriate responders, not a commitment to continue despite nonresponse or a new serious complication. Explain that the evidence concerns a selected short-term survival benefit rather than a guaranteed cure or lasting benefit from steroids alone.

bodies.heading: Match the alternative drug and route deliberately
bodies.body: For an eligible patient who cannot take oral medication, ACG describes IV methylprednisolone 32 mg/day as an alternative. This is a different drug-dose-route combination from oral prednisolone 40 mg/day. Verify the exact product and order with pharmacy and the prescribing team; do not copy the oral number into an IV order by assumption. Reconcile the indication, route and administration plan when the patient can resume oral treatment. Neither a route change nor an adjunct such as NAC removes the need for eligibility and response assessment.

bodies.heading: Monitor safety throughout corticosteroid exposure
bodies.body: Continue surveillance for infection, including fungal infection, and follow glucose control, bleeding, kidney function, mental status, liver trajectory and intake. A reassuring earlier response does not erase a newly developed hazard. New infection, gastrointestinal bleeding or organ deterioration requires prompt clinical assessment and reconsideration of continued treatment. Do not prescribe prophylactic antibiotics universally solely because severe AH or steroid treatment is present; active infection and separate cirrhosis-related prevention indications have their own management plans. Nutrition and AUD care continue alongside the steroid plan.

bodies.heading: Schedule a dynamic response assessment
bodies.body: Lille assesses early response after corticosteroid treatment has begun, unlike the baseline severity scores. Arrange calculation at day 4 or day 7 using the corresponding validated timing and a verified calculator. Check the treatment start date, baseline and follow-up bilirubin, age, baseline albumin, PT and renal information, and the units the calculator requires. A single bilirubin value or a pretreatment Lille estimate does not replace this dynamic assessment. Document who will obtain the follow-up results and act on the score; do not wait until the planned four-week course ends to discover nonresponse.

bodies.heading: Stop nonresponse and handle the boundary carefully
bodies.body: ACG key concept 27 and its official guideline summary recommend stopping corticosteroids in nonresponders with Lille greater than 0.45 at day 4 or 7. A verified score of 0.58 therefore supports stopping the AH steroid course while continuing other care and reassessing the patient. Some guideline diagrams and earlier guidance use at least 0.45 at the boundary. If a result is reported only as 0.45 after rounding, verify the unrounded score, calculation and liver-team protocol rather than declaring response or nonresponse from that display alone. A value clearly below the cutoff supports response assessment but does not guarantee safety or survival.

bodies.heading: Plan the end of the course with the prescriber
bodies.body: For a patient who responds and remains suitable for treatment, continue only the clinician-directed course with ongoing reassessment. At the planned end, provide a clear prescribing and follow-up plan. ACG states that evidence does not establish a benefit of rapid versus slow tapering after the four-week AH course; do not invent one mandatory taper for every patient. The liver team must reconcile the individual treatment history, clinical state and any other steroid indication. A response score is not permission for indefinite therapy or for a patient to change the regimen without guidance.

bodies.heading: Continue care when steroids stop or cannot be used
bodies.body: Stopping an ineffective or unsafe AH steroid course does not end care. Continue nutrition, alcohol cessation and AUD treatment, infection management and organ support. ACG recommends against pentoxifylline for severe AH, including its use as a supposed rescue for steroid nonresponse. Discuss specialist assessment, appropriate clinical-trial options and timely transplant evaluation for highly selected patients whose severe AH is unresponsive to medical management. Supportive and goals-of-care discussions should reflect clinical urgency, eligibility and patient preferences; neither a high score nor nonresponse alone dictates one outcome.

check.question: An adult who responded to the prescribed four-week AH corticosteroid course is preparing for discharge. A handoff says every patient must use the same slow taper, regardless of treatment history. What is the best response?
choices: Obtain an individualized end-of-course plan from the prescriber; ACG does not establish a benefit of rapid versus slow tapering after this course.
Extend corticosteroids indefinitely because a favorable Lille score guarantees continuing benefit.
Tell the patient to double the daily dose whenever jaundice returns.
Ignore the treatment history because one taper schedule is proven best for every patient.
check.rationale: ACG does not identify evidence favoring rapid over slow tapering after the four-week AH regimen. The prescribing team should reconcile the individual course, clinical condition and any other steroid indication and provide clear instructions and follow-up. A response score does not justify indefinite treatment, unsupervised dose changes or a universal taper claim.

alcohol-associated-liver-disease-077.question: An adult with a compatible severe-AH diagnosis has an original MELD score of 52. A learner assumes that greater severity guarantees greater corticosteroid benefit. Which correction best matches the 2024 ACG guideline?
choices: MELD above 50 warrants careful specialist risk-benefit assessment; greater severity does not guarantee greater steroid benefit.
Double the usual corticosteroid dose because benefit always increases with MELD.
The score of 52 makes contraindication screening unnecessary.
A MELD of 52 is below the severe-AH threshold.
alcohol-associated-liver-disease-077.rationale: ACG defines severe AH with original MELD greater than 20, identifies the greatest corticosteroid benefit in the 25 to 39 range and urges careful risk-benefit consideration above 50. A score of 52 signals very severe illness, not guaranteed benefit, automatic dose escalation or removal of eligibility assessment.

alcohol-associated-liver-disease-078.question: For a patient being evaluated for AH, patient PT is 18 seconds, laboratory control PT 12 seconds and total bilirubin 12 mg/dL. Using modified Maddrey DF = 4.6 × (patient PT − control PT) + bilirubin, what is the result?
alcohol-associated-liver-disease-078.rationale: The PT difference is 18 − 12 = 6 seconds. Multiply by 4.6 to obtain 27.6, then add bilirubin 12 mg/dL: mDF = 39.6. Omitting bilirubin gives 27.6; using patient PT without subtracting the control gives 94.8. The result exceeds the historical threshold of at least 32, but does not prove the diagnosis or establish steroid eligibility by itself.

alcohol-associated-liver-disease-079.question: A proposed mDF calculation uses INR in place of the PT difference because the laboratory control PT is missing. Which response is best?
choices: Obtain the appropriate laboratory control PT and confirm patient PT in seconds and bilirubin in mg/dL before calculating.
Use INR directly because it is numerically interchangeable with seconds.
Set the missing control PT to zero without checking the laboratory.
Omit bilirubin and label the result a complete mDF.
alcohol-associated-liver-disease-079.rationale: Modified Maddrey DF uses 4.6 × (patient PT − laboratory control PT) + total bilirubin, with PT in seconds and bilirubin in mg/dL. INR cannot be substituted numerically for the PT difference. A missing input should be obtained or clarified rather than invented; leaving out bilirubin produces a different, incomplete calculation.

alcohol-associated-liver-disease-080.question: An adult with severe AH is eligible for corticosteroids, can take oral medication and has a documented early response-review plan. Which oral regimen is described in the 2024 ACG guidance?
choices: Prednisolone 40 mg daily with a planned four-week course if response and safety permit.
Prednisolone 40 mg once weekly without interim assessment.
Prednisolone indefinitely after one dose, regardless of response.
Pentoxifylline as the guideline-recommended equivalent substitute.
alcohol-associated-liver-disease-080.rationale: Prednisolone 40 mg/day for four weeks is the commonly studied oral regimen. ACG also describes prednisone 40 mg/day, while generally favoring the more extensively studied prednisolone. Nonresponse or a new contraindication can change the plan, and pentoxifylline is not recommended for severe AH.

alcohol-associated-liver-disease-081.question: An otherwise eligible adult with severe AH cannot take oral medication. Which alternative drug-dose-route combination does ACG describe?
choices: Methylprednisolone 32 mg IV daily within the specialist treatment plan.
Methylprednisolone 40 mg IV daily solely by copying the oral prednisolone dose.
Prednisolone 40 mg orally despite inability to use the oral route.
An oral supplement as an interchangeable steroid preparation.
alcohol-associated-liver-disease-081.rationale: ACG describes IV methylprednisolone 32 mg/day for patients unable to take oral medication. The exact drug, route and order must be verified. Copying the oral prednisolone dose into an IV methylprednisolone order without review is not the specified alternative; oral medication or a supplement does not address this route requirement.

alcohol-associated-liver-disease-082.question: A patient with severe AH has active, untreated hepatitis B infection. What does the ACG corticosteroid eligibility framework require?
choices: Address the untreated infection and obtain specialist reassessment before starting the AH corticosteroid course.
Start corticosteroids automatically because any high MELD overrides untreated infection.
Ignore hepatitis B because only bacterial infections affect steroid eligibility.
Treat all patients with any past hepatitis B exposure as permanently ineligible, regardless of current status.
alcohol-associated-liver-disease-082.rationale: ACG lists active infection, including untreated hepatitis B infection, among contraindications to corticosteroids in AH. Current infection status and its management require specialist review. Severity does not override the hazard, and this statement is not a permanent exclusion based on any historical exposure alone.

alcohol-associated-liver-disease-083.question: A patient with severe AH has uncontrolled diabetes and ongoing gastrointestinal bleeding. The proposed steroid plan cites only an elevated mDF. Which action is best?
choices: Manage the unresolved hazards and reassess corticosteroid eligibility with the liver team.
Start corticosteroids immediately because mDF overrides every contraindication.
Ignore glucose and bleeding once a severity score is available.
Increase steroid exposure to treat the bleeding directly.
alcohol-associated-liver-disease-083.rationale: Uncontrolled diabetes and gastrointestinal bleeding are contraindications in the ACG AH corticosteroid framework. Control or address these problems and reassess the complete clinical state. A severity score alone does not establish eligibility, and steroids do not substitute for urgent bleeding management.

alcohol-associated-liver-disease-084.question: Before starting an eligible severe-AH corticosteroid course, the team asks when to assess Lille response. Which plan matches ACG guidance?
choices: Arrange the corresponding Lille assessment at treatment day 4 or day 7 using verified baseline and follow-up data.
Calculate one pretreatment Lille score and omit all follow-up bilirubin measurements.
Wait until day 28 before evaluating treatment response for the first time.
Use any isolated bilirubin result without confirming treatment timing or the other inputs.
alcohol-associated-liver-disease-084.rationale: Lille is a dynamic response assessment after corticosteroids begin. ACG supports assessment at day 4 or day 7. Verify the timing, baseline and follow-up bilirubin, other required inputs and calculator units, and assign someone to act on the result. A pretreatment score or isolated value cannot replace the intended response review.

alcohol-associated-liver-disease-085.question: An AH patient has a verified day-7 Lille score of 0.58. Which action follows ACG key concept 27?
choices: Stop the AH corticosteroid course for nonresponse while continuing specialist and supportive care.
Continue automatically to day 28 because every started course must be completed.
Double the steroid dose until the Lille score becomes zero.
End nutrition, infection surveillance and AUD care when steroids stop.
alcohol-associated-liver-disease-085.rationale: A Lille score greater than 0.45 identifies nonresponse in ACG key concept 27 and supports discontinuing corticosteroids. The supplied value 0.58 clearly exceeds that cutoff. Stopping an ineffective course does not end nutrition, infection management, organ support, AUD care or specialist assessment.

alcohol-associated-liver-disease-086.question: A report displays a Lille score of 0.45 rounded to two decimal places. Guideline materials differ at the exact boundary. Which response is most appropriate?
choices: Verify the unrounded score, calculation and applicable liver-team protocol before making the boundary decision.
Declare definite response solely because the displayed number is not above 0.45.
Declare definite nonresponse solely from the rounded display without checking its underlying value.
Ignore the score and continue indefinitely without reassessment.
alcohol-associated-liver-disease-086.rationale: ACG key concept 27 and its official highlights use greater than 0.45, while some diagrams and earlier guidance use at least 0.45. A rounded display can obscure which side of the boundary the calculated result occupies. Verify the complete calculation and local specialist protocol rather than forcing a treatment decision from the rounded display alone.

alcohol-associated-liver-disease-087.question: A patient had a favorable day-4 Lille score of 0.19 but develops new gastrointestinal bleeding during the AH steroid course. What is the best approach?
choices: Urgently assess and manage the bleeding and reconsider continued corticosteroid eligibility, despite the earlier response.
Continue automatically because the earlier Lille score guarantees steroid safety.
Ignore bleeding until the planned four-week course ends.
Use the favorable Lille score to exclude every new complication.
alcohol-associated-liver-disease-087.rationale: A favorable response score does not remove a new contraindication or guarantee safety. Gastrointestinal bleeding requires urgent assessment and management, with reconsideration of the AH steroid plan. Continue the rest of the appropriate care while the liver team reviews the evolving condition.

alcohol-associated-liver-disease-088.question: A patient is a corticosteroid nonresponder in severe AH. A handoff proposes pentoxifylline as a proven salvage replacement. Which correction best matches ACG guidance?
choices: Pentoxifylline is not recommended; continue appropriate support and specialist assessment of further options.
Pentoxifylline is a proven salvage therapy for every steroid nonresponder.
Stop all nutrition and AUD care because no steroid response means no further care is useful.
Guarantee transplant solely from the Lille score without evaluating eligibility.
alcohol-associated-liver-disease-088.rationale: ACG recommends against pentoxifylline for severe AH and describes lack of efficacy as steroid-nonresponse salvage. Ongoing nutrition, AUD treatment, infection management and organ support remain necessary. Specialists may assess appropriate trials and early transplant evaluation for highly selected patients; neither nonresponse nor one score guarantees transplant eligibility.

False: INR is not a duration in seconds.
False: zero control invents missing input.
False: omitting bilirubin not complete mDF.
wholeBankQuestions.singleBestAnswerReview: Modified Maddrey DF uses 4.6 × (patient PT − laboratory control PT) + total bilirubin, with PT in seconds and bilirubin in mg/dL. INR cannot be substituted numerically for the PT difference. A missing input should be obtained or clarified rather than invented; leaving out bilirubin produces a different, incomplete calculation.

wholeObject.question: An adult with severe AH is eligible for corticosteroids, can take oral medication and has a documented early response-review plan. Which oral regimen is described in the 2024 ACG guidance?
choices: Prednisolone 40 mg daily with a planned four-week course if response and safety permit.
Prednisolone 40 mg once weekly without interim assessment.
Prednisolone indefinitely after one dose, regardless of response.
Pentoxifylline as the guideline-recommended equivalent substitute.
wholeObject.rationale: Prednisolone 40 mg/day for four weeks is the commonly studied oral regimen. ACG also describes prednisone 40 mg/day, while generally favoring the more extensively studied prednisolone. Nonresponse or a new contraindication can change the plan, and pentoxifylline is not recommended for severe AH.

wholeChoiceReview: Correct: oral prednisolone daily 40 mg, planned four weeks only if response/safety permit.
False: weekly schedule not stated AH regimen.
False: indefinite treatment unsupported.
False: PTX not equivalent guideline substitute.
wholeBankQuestions.singleBestAnswerReview: Prednisolone 40 mg/day for four weeks is the commonly studied oral regimen. ACG also describes prednisone 40 mg/day, while generally favoring the more extensively studied prednisolone. Nonresponse or a new contraindication can change the plan, and pentoxifylline is not recommended for severe AH.

wholeObject.question: An otherwise eligible adult with severe AH cannot take oral medication. Which alternative drug-dose-route combination does ACG describe?
choices: Methylprednisolone 32 mg IV daily within the specialist treatment plan.
Methylprednisolone 40 mg IV daily solely by copying the oral prednisolone dose.
Prednisolone 40 mg orally despite inability to use the oral route.
An oral supplement as an interchangeable steroid preparation.
wholeObject.rationale: ACG describes IV methylprednisolone 32 mg/day for patients unable to take oral medication. The exact drug, route and order must be verified. Copying the oral prednisolone dose into an IV methylprednisolone order without review is not the specified alternative; oral medication or a supplement does not address this route requirement.

wholeChoiceReview: Correct: IV methylprednisolone 32 mg/day if oral impossible.
False: unreviewed copy of oral 40 mg is not specified IV alternative.
False: oral route does not solve inability to take oral.
False: supplement not steroid preparation substitute.
wholeBankQuestions.singleBestAnswerReview: ACG describes IV methylprednisolone 32 mg/day for patients unable to take oral medication. The exact drug, route and order must be verified. Copying the oral prednisolone dose into an IV methylprednisolone order without review is not the specified alternative; oral medication or a supplement does not address this route requirement.

wholeObject.question: A patient with severe AH has active, untreated hepatitis B infection. What does the ACG corticosteroid eligibility framework require?
choices: Address the untreated infection and obtain specialist reassessment before starting the AH corticosteroid course.
Start corticosteroids automatically because any high MELD overrides untreated infection.
Ignore hepatitis B because only bacterial infections affect steroid eligibility.
Treat all patients with any past hepatitis B exposure as permanently ineligible, regardless of current status.
wholeObject.rationale: ACG lists active infection, including untreated hepatitis B infection, among contraindications to corticosteroids in AH. Current infection status and its management require specialist review. Severity does not override the hazard, and this statement is not a permanent exclusion based on any historical exposure alone.

wholeChoiceReview: Correct: address active untreated HBV and specialist eligibility review.
False: MELD not override infection hazard.
False: active untreated viral infection explicitly included.
False: any historical exposure not universal permanent exclusion.
wholeBankQuestions.singleBestAnswerReview: ACG lists active infection, including untreated hepatitis B infection, among contraindications to corticosteroids in AH. Current infection status and its management require specialist review. Severity does not override the hazard, and this statement is not a permanent exclusion based on any historical exposure alone.

wholeObject.question: A patient with severe AH has uncontrolled diabetes and ongoing gastrointestinal bleeding. The proposed steroid plan cites only an elevated mDF. Which action is best?
choices: Manage the unresolved hazards and reassess corticosteroid eligibility with the liver team.
Start corticosteroids immediately because mDF overrides every contraindication.
Ignore glucose and bleeding once a severity score is available.
Increase steroid exposure to treat the bleeding directly.
wholeObject.rationale: Uncontrolled diabetes and gastrointestinal bleeding are contraindications in the ACG AH corticosteroid framework. Control or address these problems and reassess the complete clinical state. A severity score alone does not establish eligibility, and steroids do not substitute for urgent bleeding management.

wholeChoiceReview: Correct: manage uncontrolled diabetes/GI bleeding and reassess.
False: mDF not override contraindications.
False: score does not render glucose/bleeding irrelevant.
False: steroid escalation not bleeding treatment.
wholeBankQuestions.singleBestAnswerReview: Uncontrolled diabetes and gastrointestinal bleeding are contraindications in the ACG AH corticosteroid framework. Control or address these problems and reassess the complete clinical state. A severity score alone does not establish eligibility, and steroids do not substitute for urgent bleeding management.

wholeObject.question: Before starting an eligible severe-AH corticosteroid course, the team asks when to assess Lille response. Which plan matches ACG guidance?
choices: Arrange the corresponding Lille assessment at treatment day 4 or day 7 using verified baseline and follow-up data.
Calculate one pretreatment Lille score and omit all follow-up bilirubin measurements.
Wait until day 28 before evaluating treatment response for the first time.
Use any isolated bilirubin result without confirming treatment timing or the other inputs.
wholeObject.rationale: Lille is a dynamic response assessment after corticosteroids begin. ACG supports assessment at day 4 or day 7. Verify the timing, baseline and follow-up bilirubin, other required inputs and calculator units, and assign someone to act on the result. A pretreatment score or isolated value cannot replace the intended response review.

wholeChoiceReview: Correct: treatment day 4 or 7 corresponding validated timing and data.
False: pretreatment score not dynamic response review.
False: day 28-only review delays necessary assessment.
False: isolated bilirubin without timing/inputs insufficient.
wholeBankQuestions.singleBestAnswerReview: Lille is a dynamic response assessment after corticosteroids begin. ACG supports assessment at day 4 or day 7. Verify the timing, baseline and follow-up bilirubin, other required inputs and calculator units, and assign someone to act on the result. A pretreatment score or isolated value cannot replace the intended response review.

wholeObject.question: An AH patient has a verified day-7 Lille score of 0.58. Which action follows ACG key concept 27?
choices: Stop the AH corticosteroid course for nonresponse while continuing specialist and supportive care.
Continue automatically to day 28 because every started course must be completed.
Double the steroid dose until the Lille score becomes zero.
End nutrition, infection surveillance and AUD care when steroids stop.
wholeObject.rationale: A Lille score greater than 0.45 identifies nonresponse in ACG key concept 27 and supports discontinuing corticosteroids. The supplied value 0.58 clearly exceeds that cutoff. Stopping an ineffective course does not end nutrition, infection management, organ support, AUD care or specialist assessment.

wholeChoiceReview: Correct: stop nonresponse AH steroid course, maintain support.
False: planned 28 days not unconditional.
False: automatic doubling unsupported.
False: stopping steroid does not end other care.
wholeBankQuestions.singleBestAnswerReview: A Lille score greater than 0.45 identifies nonresponse in ACG key concept 27 and supports discontinuing corticosteroids. The supplied value 0.58 clearly exceeds that cutoff. Stopping an ineffective course does not end nutrition, infection management, organ support, AUD care or specialist assessment.

wholeObject.question: A report displays a Lille score of 0.45 rounded to two decimal places. Guideline materials differ at the exact boundary. Which response is most appropriate?
choices: Verify the unrounded score, calculation and applicable liver-team protocol before making the boundary decision.
Declare definite response solely because the displayed number is not above 0.45.
Declare definite nonresponse solely from the rounded display without checking its underlying value.
Ignore the score and continue indefinitely without reassessment.
wholeObject.rationale: ACG key concept 27 and its official highlights use greater than 0.45, while some diagrams and earlier guidance use at least 0.45. A rounded display can obscure which side of the boundary the calculated result occupies. Verify the complete calculation and local specialist protocol rather than forcing a treatment decision from the rounded display alone.

wholeChoiceReview: Correct: unrounded value/calculation and applicable protocol review.
False: rounded display does not prove response.
False: rounded display does not independently prove nonresponse.
False: no indefinite unreviewed exposure.
wholeBankQuestions.singleBestAnswerReview: ACG key concept 27 and its official highlights use greater than 0.45, while some diagrams and earlier guidance use at least 0.45. A rounded display can obscure which side of the boundary the calculated result occupies. Verify the complete calculation and local specialist protocol rather than forcing a treatment decision from the rounded display alone.

wholeObject.question: A patient had a favorable day-4 Lille score of 0.19 but develops new gastrointestinal bleeding during the AH steroid course. What is the best approach?
choices: Urgently assess and manage the bleeding and reconsider continued corticosteroid eligibility, despite the earlier response.
Continue automatically because the earlier Lille score guarantees steroid safety.
Ignore bleeding until the planned four-week course ends.
Use the favorable Lille score to exclude every new complication.
wholeObject.rationale: A favorable response score does not remove a new contraindication or guarantee safety. Gastrointestinal bleeding requires urgent assessment and management, with reconsideration of the AH steroid plan. Continue the rest of the appropriate care while the liver team reviews the evolving condition.

wholeChoiceReview: Correct: urgent bleeding care and reconsider treatment despite earlier low Lille.
False: response does not guarantee safety.
False: bleeding cannot wait for course end.
False: earlier response cannot exclude new complications.
wholeBankQuestions.singleBestAnswerReview: A favorable response score does not remove a new contraindication or guarantee safety. Gastrointestinal bleeding requires urgent assessment and management, with reconsideration of the AH steroid plan. Continue the rest of the appropriate care while the liver team reviews the evolving condition.

wholeObject.question: A patient is a corticosteroid nonresponder in severe AH. A handoff proposes pentoxifylline as a proven salvage replacement. Which correction best matches ACG guidance?
choices: Pentoxifylline is not recommended; continue appropriate support and specialist assessment of further options.
Pentoxifylline is a proven salvage therapy for every steroid nonresponder.
Stop all nutrition and AUD care because no steroid response means no further care is useful.
Guarantee transplant solely from the Lille score without evaluating eligibility.
wholeObject.rationale: ACG recommends against pentoxifylline for severe AH and describes lack of efficacy as steroid-nonresponse salvage. Ongoing nutrition, AUD treatment, infection management and organ support remain necessary. Specialists may assess appropriate trials and early transplant evaluation for highly selected patients; neither nonresponse nor one score guarantees transplant eligibility.

wholeChoiceReview: Correct: PTX not recommended salvage, maintain support/specialist review.
False: no proven universal salvage.
False: nonresponse not reason to abandon nutrition/AUD care.
False: score does not guarantee LT eligibility.
wholeBankQuestions.singleBestAnswerReview: ACG recommends against pentoxifylline for severe AH and describes lack of efficacy as steroid-nonresponse salvage. Ongoing nutrition, AUD treatment, infection management and organ support remain necessary. Specialists may assess appropriate trials and early transplant evaluation for highly selected patients; neither nonresponse nor one score guarantees transplant eligibility.
